cards.title: Five freedoms, one sentence
cards.text: One sentence in the U.S. Constitution protects five big freedoms. It is called the First Amendment. Can you guess any of the five?

cards.question: Some students wore black armbands to school as a silent protest, and they were suspended. What do you think the Supreme Court said?

options.text: The students keep free speech at school
Students have no free speech at school
Armbands are clothes, so they don't count

cards.reveal: The Court sided with the students, 7 votes to 2. Students do not lose their free speech rights "at the schoolhouse gate."

cards.title: The five freedoms
cards.text: The First Amendment protects freedom of religion, speech, and the press. It also protects the right to gather peacefully and the right to petition, which means asking the government to fix a problem.
cards.example: It became part of the Constitution in 1791, as part of the Bill of Rights.

cards.title: The armband story
cards.text: During the Vietnam War, some students at a public school in Des Moines, Iowa, wore black armbands to school. It was a silent protest against the war. The principal had warned them they would be suspended, and they were.

cards.title: The Supreme Court decides
cards.text: The students' parents went to court. In 1969, the Supreme Court sided with the students, 7 votes to 2. It said students do not lose their rights to free speech "at the schoolhouse gate."

cards.title: The other side
cards.text: Two justices disagreed. They said school is for learning and the armbands were a distraction. They thought schools should have a lot of power to keep classes calm and focused.
cards.example: Both sides cared about something important: free speech, and a good place to learn.

why.q: Why might a fair person agree with parts of both sides?
why.a: Both sides cared about something important: free speech, and a good place to learn.

cards.prompt: In "Three Branches, One Team" you learned that courts can check other parts of government. How did a court do that in the armband case?
cards.model: The Supreme Court sided with the students against their public school. A court checked a part of government.

cards.question: Where should a school draw the line between letting students speak up and keeping class focused?
nudges: What kinds of speech help a school?
What would make speech too disruptive?

questions.q: Which of these is one of the five First Amendment freedoms?

options.text: Freedom of the press
options.why: Yes! Also religion, speech, peaceful gathering, and petition.

options.text: Freedom from homework
options.why: Nice try! That is not in the Constitution.

options.text: Freedom to drive at any age
options.why: Not one of the five. Driving rules come from state laws.

questions.q: What did the students in Des Moines do?

options.text: Wore black armbands as a silent protest
options.why: Right. They were suspended, and the case went to the Supreme Court.

options.text: Wrote a newspaper
Skipped school
options.why: They went to school wearing armbands.

questions.q: What did the two justices who disagreed think?

options.text: Schools need power to keep class calm and focused.
options.why: Yes. They worried about distraction from learning.

options.text: Students should never be allowed in school.
options.why: No. They wanted schools to keep order.

options.text: The armbands should be required for everyone.
options.why: No. They thought the school could ban them.
